name: Srimoorthy Perumal Temple, Salagramam (Muktinath)
deity: Vishnu as Muktinath, the lord of liberation — Srimoorthy of the Divya Desam lists — revered with Sridevi and Bhudevi and worshipped as the Salagrama
period: A Divya Desam of Vada Nadu in the high Himalaya, sung by Thirumangai Alvar and Periyalvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham
dynasty: Sacred site of great antiquity; the present temple credited to Queen Subarna Prabha, c. 1815
summary: High in the Himalaya of Nepal, at the foot of the Thorong La, Vishnu is worshipped as Muktinath, the lord of liberation — the only Divya Desam beyond India, and a place revered by Buddhists too.

sections.history: Salagramam, the Divya Desam of Muktinath, lies in Mustang, Nepal, and is the only one of the 108 beyond India; it belongs to Vada Nadu. Thirumangai Alvar sang it in a decad of ten pasurams, Periya Thirumozhi 1.5, and tradition says he sang from the nearest place he could reach rather than the shrine itself. Periyalvar names the lord Salagramamudaiya Nambi. The present pagoda-style temple is credited to Queen Subarna Prabha of Nepal, around 1815, but the image and the site are far older, and the Puranas already link the Salagrama stones to the Gandaki. Muktinath is also revered by Buddhists, who know it as Chumig Gyatsa, the Hundred Waters, and honour it as a sacred place of Avalokiteshvara.
sections.architecture: At about 3,700 metres, at the foot of the Thorong La pass near Ranipauwa, stands a small pagoda-style shrine with a golden roof. Behind it curves a wall of 108 water spouts, the Muktidhara, carved in the form of animal heads, where pilgrims bathe beneath the icy streams. Two ponds lie in front of the temple, the Mukti Kunda and another named Saraswati Kunda. The whole complex is modest in scale and austere in setting, its beauty owed to the mountains around it.
sections.legends: The Salagrama, an ammonite fossil found in the Kali Gandaki, is worshipped as Vishnu himself, and Damodar Kunda is regarded as a source of the sacred stones and of the Gandaki. Another tradition tells of Vrinda, wife of Jalandhara, who cursed Vishnu to become stone; Vishnu is worshipped as the Salagrama, and the Tulasi leaf is never parted from his worship. Versions differ, and one holds Muktinath to be the place where the lord was freed of the curse. Tibetan Buddhists associate the site with Avalokiteshvara and with Guru Rinpoche, Padmasambhava.
sections.festivals: No single festival defines Muktinath; its life is the pilgrimage itself, concentrated in the open seasons of spring and autumn, when the high passes are passable. The central observance is bathing beneath the 108 spouts and in the two kundas. Hindu and Buddhist pilgrims share the sacred ground side by side. Confirm conditions and any observances locally.
sections.experience: Few journeys in the Divya Desam tradition demand as much as this one, and few reward the pilgrim so. Take the time for altitude acclimatisation, move slowly in the thin air, and dress for cold water and wind. Bathe beneath the 108 spouts if you are able, then offer respects at the shrine of Muktinath. Hindu and Buddhist devotees pray here together, and the stillness of the high valley suits both.

visit.timings: Open to pilgrims through the day; access depends on season and weather, and the high season is spring and autumn. Confirm current conditions locally before travelling.
visit.dressCode: Modest dress is expected, with warm layers for the altitude; footwear is removed before entering the shrine. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: From Pokhara, travel to Jomsom by air or by road via Beni, then continue by road to Ranipauwa, near the village sometimes itself called Muktinath, and make a short climb to the temple. Plan for gradual acclimatisation to the altitude, and confirm road and flight conditions locally.
